title: Cookies and Browser Storage
path: Web Interview Prep/Cookies and Browser Storage.md
body:
Interview prep note. See [[Cookies]] for the course-notes version.

## Core Facts to Know

- A cookie is set by the server with the `Set-Cookie` response header.
- A cookie is stored by the browser, on your machine.
- The browser attaches the `Cookie` header automatically on every matching request.
- Sending a cookie requires no JS code.
- A [[Session Cookie]] has no expiry and is deleted when the browser closes.
- A [[Persistent Cookie]] has `Expires` or `Max-Age` and survives a restart.
- Cookie lifetime is enforced by the browser.
- `HttpOnly` means page JS cannot read the cookie.
- `HttpOnly` defends against [[XSS]] token theft.
- `Secure` means the cookie is never sent over plain HTTP.
- `SameSite` controls whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests.
- `SameSite` is the core [[CSRF]] defense.
- Cookies must be treated as untrusted user input.
- An [[Origin]] is scheme + host + port together.
- `https://app.example.com` and `https://api.example.com` are different origins.
- The [[Same-Origin Policy]] is enforced entirely by the browser, never by the server.
- [[CORS]] headers are set by the server, but the block/allow decision is made by the browser.
- A CORS-blocked request may already have reached and executed on the server.
- A [[Preflight Request]] is an automatic `OPTIONS` request sent by the browser.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is the main CORS response header.
- [[localStorage]] persists indefinitely and is never auto-sent to the server.
- [[sessionStorage]] is scoped to one tab and cleared when that tab closes.
- Both localStorage and sessionStorage are read and written explicitly by your JS.
- Cookies auto-attach, which makes them useful for auth but a CSRF risk.
- localStorage and sessionStorage never auto-attach, so they carry no direct CSRF risk.
- A JWT in localStorage is more exposed to XSS theft, because your own JS can read it.

## Core analogy: A wristband at a venue

A cookie is a wristband the venue (server) puts on you the first time you enter. Every time you walk up to a different counter inside the same venue (make another request to the same origin), you show the wristband again automatically. The venue decides what's written on it, how long it's valid, and whether other venues can scan it.

This is how a [[Stateless Protocol]] like [[HTTP]] fakes having state. The browser's collection of these is the [[Cookie Jar]].

## Cookies, mapped

| Wristband concept | Cookie term | Where it happens |
|---|---|---|
| Venue puts the wristband on you at check-in | `Set-Cookie` response header | Sent by **their machine**, stored by **your machine** (the browser) |
| You don't consciously present the wristband, it's shown automatically | `Cookie` header sent on every matching request | Attached automatically by **your browser**, no JS code required |
| A wristband cut off at closing time vs. one stamped with an expiry date | Session cookie (deleted when browser closes) vs. persistent cookie (`Expires`/`Max-Age`) | Lifetime enforced by **your browser** |
| A wristband only staff can read, not other guests | `HttpOnly` — JS on the page cannot read/copy it, defends against XSS token theft | Enforced by **your browser**, restricting **your own page's JS** |
| Only shown over an encrypted line | `Secure` — never sent over plain HTTP | Enforced by **your browser** |
| Rule about showing the wristband when arriving from a different venue's link | `SameSite` (`Strict`/`Lax`/`None`) — core CSRF defense | Enforced by **your browser**, set by **their server** |

## Same-origin policy and CORS

Analogy: a wristband from Venue A means nothing at Venue B, and Venue B's staff ([[JavaScript]]) can't even look inside Venue A's booth unless Venue A explicitly allows it.

| Wristband concept                                                             | Term                                                                                              | Where it's enforced                                                                                                                                                               |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Scheme + host + port together define "the same venue"                         | Origin, e.g. `https://app.example.com` vs `https://api.example.com` are different origins | Defined and checked by **your browser**                                                                                                                                           |
| Staff from one venue can't look inside another's booth by default             | Same-origin policy                                                                                | Enforced entirely by **your browser** — never by the server                                                                                                                       |
| Venue A explicitly hands out a pass allowing Venue B's staff to look          | CORS — `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and related headers                                          | Header set by **their server**; the resulting block/allow decision is enforced by **your browser** — the request itself may already have reached and executed on **their server** |
| A guard asking "if I let this in, will you allow it?" before the real request | Preflight — an automatic `OPTIONS` request                                                        | Sent by **your browser** automatically, answered by **their server**                                                                                                              |

## Other browser storage, in the same analogy family

| Wristband concept | Term | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| A locker that persists indefinitely, only you can open it | `localStorage` — never auto-sent to the server | **Your machine only**, read/written explicitly by **your JS** |
| The same locker, but emptied when you leave this specific room | `sessionStorage` — cleared when the tab closes | **Your machine only**, scoped to one tab |
| The wristband is shown automatically everywhere; the locker key is never shown to anyone unless you hand it over | Practical distinction: cookies auto-attach (useful for auth, but a CSRF risk); `localStorage`/`sessionStorage` never auto-attach (no CSRF risk from them directly, but JWT-in-localStorage is more exposed to XSS theft since your own JS can read it) | Both live on **your machine**; the difference is who automatically transmits them |
